title: The Point That Shows the Unit Rate

steps.body: The point **(1, k)** always shows the unit rate directly — when x = 1, y = k × 1 = k. Find where the line crosses x = 1, and its height IS the unit rate.
Plot the unit-rate point for k = 3.

widget.prompt: A line has unit rate of 3. Plot the point that shows this unit rate directly.

pointErrors.feedback: That's (3, 1) — slots swapped. The unit-rate point has x=1: plot (1, 3).

widget.missFeedback: The unit rate point always has x=1: plot (1, 3).
widget.successFeedback: Yes — (1, 3) directly shows the unit rate of 3.

predict.prompt: A line's unit rate is 3. At which x-value does the graph show the unit rate directly?
predict.reveal: Unit rate means 'per ONE' — at x = 1 the height of the line IS the rate itself. That single point carries the whole story.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents unit rate point.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for unit rate point must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines unit rate point.

steps.body: Going the other way: if you're told the point (1, 4) is on the line, you instantly know the unit rate is 4 — no computation needed.
Read the rate from a point.

widget.prompt: The graphed point (1, 6) represents a proportional relationship. What is the unit rate?

numericErrors.feedback: 1 is the x-value. Since x=1, the y-value IS the unit rate: 6.

widget.successFeedback: Yes — (1, 6) sits on the line through the origin, so the unit rate is 6 ÷ 1 = 6.
widget.explorationFeedback: Open a stage to read the graphed point, then type the unit rate.
widget.fallbackFeedback: Since x=1, the unit rate is the y-value: 6.

steps.body: For any OTHER point (x, y) on the line, the unit rate is still y/x — the point (1, k) is just the special case where the division is instant.
Read the rate from a different point.

widget.prompt: The graphed point (4, 20) represents a proportional relationship. What is the unit rate?

numericErrors.feedback: That's 20 − 4. The unit rate is y ÷ x: 20 ÷ 4 = 5.
4 is the x-value, not the rate. The unit rate is 20 ÷ 4 = 5.

widget.successFeedback: Yes — (4, 20) sits on the line through the origin, so the unit rate is 20 ÷ 4 = 5.
widget.explorationFeedback: Open a stage to read the graphed point, then type the unit rate.

hints: The unit rate is y divided by x.

steps.body: The point (1, k) shows the unit rate directly; any other point still gives k = y/x.
takeaways: At x=1, the y-value IS the unit rate.
For any point, unit rate = y ÷ x.
This works whether you're plotting or reading a graph.
